title: Higher-order Derivatives and Applications of Derivatives
summary: Derivatives measure rates of change, and in commerce they turn cost, revenue and profit functions into marginal quantities and optimal decisions. This chapter covers second-order derivatives (explicit, implicit and parametric), marginal cost and marginal revenue, increasing and decreasing functions, and finding maxima and minima with business and geometry applications.

notes.heading: Higher-order derivatives
notes.html:
If y = f(x), the derivative dy/dx = f′(x) is the first derivative. Differentiating again gives the second derivative d2y/dx2 = f″(x) (also written y2 or y″), and so on.

Standard derivatives used: d(xn)/dx = nxn − 1; d(eax)/dx = aeax; d(log x)/dx = 1/x; d(ax)/dx = ax log a; product rule (uv)′ = u′v + uv′; quotient rule (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v2; chain rule.

Example (explicit): y = x3 − 4x2 + 7x − 2 ⇒ dy/dx = 3x2 − 8x + 7 ⇒ d2y/dx2 = 6x − 8.

Example: y = e2x + log x ⇒ y′ = 2e2x + 1/x ⇒ y″ = 4e2x − 1/x2.

Parametric form x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), and d2y/dx2 = [d/dt (dy/dx)] ÷ (dx/dt) — do not simply divide the second derivatives.

Example: x = t2, y = t3: dy/dx = 3t2/2t = 3t/2; d2y/dx2 = (3/2) ÷ (2t) = 3/(4t).

Implicit form: differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x, then differentiate the result again and substitute for y′.

notes.heading: Marginal cost and marginal revenue
notes.html:
• Total cost C(x) = fixed cost + variable cost, where x = number of units produced.
  • Average cost AC = C(x)/x. Marginal cost MC = dC/dx — approximately the cost of producing one more unit.
  • Total revenue R(x) = p · x, where p is the price per unit (often given by a demand function). Average revenue AR = R/x = p. Marginal revenue MR = dR/dx.
  • Profit P(x) = R(x) − C(x); marginal profit = dP/dx = MR − MC.
  • At maximum profit, MR = MC (first-order condition) and d2P/dx2 < 0.
  • At minimum average cost, MC = AC.

Worked Example 1. C(x) = 0.005x3 − 0.02x2 + 30x + 5000. MC = 0.015x2 − 0.04x + 30. At x = 3: MC = 0.135 − 0.12 + 30 = ₹30.015.

R(x) = 3x2 + 36x + 5 ⇒ MR = 6x + 36. At x = 5: MR = ₹66.

notes.heading: Increasing and decreasing functions
notes.html:
A function f is strictly increasing on an interval if x1 < x2 ⇒ f(x1) < f(x2), and strictly decreasing if x1 < x2 ⇒ f(x1) > f(x2).

  • f′(x) > 0 on an interval ⇒ f strictly increasing there.
  • f′(x) < 0 on an interval ⇒ f strictly decreasing there.
  • f′(x) = 0 throughout ⇒ f constant.

Method: (1) find f′(x); (2) solve f′(x) = 0 to get critical points; (3) these points split the line into intervals; (4) test the sign of f′ in each interval.

notes.heading: Maxima and minima — tests
notes.html:
A critical (stationary) point is a point c where f′(c) = 0.

  • First derivative test: if f′ changes sign from + to − at c, f has a local maximum at c; from − to +, a local minimum; no change of sign — neither (e.g. f(x) = x3 at 0).
  • Second derivative test: if f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0 ⇒ local maximum; f″(c) > 0 ⇒ local minimum; f″(c) = 0 ⇒ test fails, use the first derivative test.
  • Absolute (global) extrema on [a, b]: evaluate f at all critical points inside [a, b] and at the end points a and b; the largest value is the absolute maximum and the smallest the absolute minimum.

Steps for a word problem: (1) define the variable; (2) express the quantity to be optimised as a function of one variable (use the given condition to eliminate others); (3) differentiate and equate to 0; (4) confirm max/min with the second derivative; (5) answer the question asked, with units.

notes.heading: Worked Example 2 — intervals and local extrema
notes.html:
f(x) = 2x3 − 9x2 + 12x + 15.

f′(x) = 6x2 − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2). Critical points x = 1, 2.

IntervalSign of f′(x)Behaviour
x < 1+increasing
1 < x < 2−decreasing
x > 2+increasing

f is strictly increasing on (−∞, 1) and (2, ∞), strictly decreasing on (1, 2).

f″(x) = 12x − 18. f″(1) = −6 < 0 ⇒ local maximum, f(1) = 2 − 9 + 12 + 15 = 20. f″(2) = 6 > 0 ⇒ local minimum, f(2) = 16 − 36 + 24 + 15 = 19.

notes.heading: Worked Example 3 — maximum profit and minimum average cost
notes.html:
(a) The demand function of a product is p = 120 − 2x and the cost function is C(x) = 100 + 30x + x2. Find the output that maximises profit.

R(x) = px = 120x − 2x2. P(x) = R − C = 120x − 2x2 − 100 − 30x − x2 = −3x2 + 90x − 100.

P′(x) = −6x + 90 = 0 ⇒ x = 15. P″(x) = −6 < 0 ⇒ maximum.

Maximum profit P(15) = −675 + 1350 − 100 = ₹575 at price p = 120 − 30 = ₹90. (Check MR = 120 − 4x = 60 and MC = 30 + 2x = 60 at x = 15 ✓.)

(b) C(x) = 2x2 + 5x + 200. Find the output at which average cost is least.

AC = 2x + 5 + 200/x. d(AC)/dx = 2 − 200/x2 = 0 ⇒ x2 = 100 ⇒ x = 10 (x > 0). Second derivative 400/x3 > 0 ⇒ minimum.

Minimum AC = 20 + 5 + 20 = ₹45. MC = 4x + 5 = 45 at x = 10, confirming MC = AC at minimum average cost.

notes.heading: Worked Example 4 — an optimisation in geometry
notes.html:
An open box is made from a square sheet of side 18 cm by cutting equal squares of side x cm from each corner and folding up the sides. Find x for maximum volume.

V(x) = x(18 − 2x)2, 0 < x < 9.

V′(x) = (18 − 2x)2 + x · 2(18 − 2x)(−2) = (18 − 2x)(18 − 2x − 4x) = (18 − 2x)(18 − 6x).

V′ = 0 ⇒ x = 9 (gives V = 0, rejected) or x = 3.

V″(x) = 24x − 144 (from V = 4x3 − 72x2 + 324x, V′ = 12x2 − 144x + 324). V″(3) = 72 − 144 = −72 < 0 ⇒ maximum.

x = 3 cm, maximum volume = 3 × 122 = 432 cm3.

notes.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
notes.html:
• Taking d2y/dx2 = (d2y/dt2)/(d2x/dt2) in parametric form.
  • Confusing average cost C/x with marginal cost dC/dx.
  • Maximising revenue instead of profit when the question asks for profit.
  • Forgetting to reject critical points outside the meaningful domain (negative output, zero volume).
  • Stating a maximum without the second-derivative (or sign-change) check.
  • Thinking f′(c) = 0 always gives an extremum — x3 at 0 is a counter-example.
  • Giving the value of x when the question asks for the maximum value of the function (or vice versa).

keyTerms.definition: The derivative of the first derivative, d<sup>2</sup>y/dx<sup>2</sup>; it measures how the rate of change itself changes.
MC = dC/dx, the approximate cost of producing one additional unit.
MR = dR/dx, the approximate extra revenue from selling one additional unit.
AC = C(x)/x, total cost per unit.
f with f(x<sub>1</sub>) < f(x<sub>2</sub>) whenever x<sub>1</sub> < x<sub>2</sub>; guaranteed when f′ > 0.
A value f(c) greater than or equal to all nearby values; f′ changes from + to − at c.
A value f(c) less than or equal to all nearby values; f′ changes from − to + at c.
The greatest/least value of f on its whole domain or a given closed interval.

questions.q: Find the local maximum and local minimum values of f(x) = 2x<sup>3</sup> − 9x<sup>2</sup> + 12x + 15.
The total cost of producing x units is C(x) = 2x<sup>2</sup> + 5x + 200. Find the output at which average cost is minimum and show that at this output MC = AC.
questions.answerHtml:
AC = C/x = 2x + 5 + 200/x.

d(AC)/dx = 2 − 200/x2 = 0 ⇒ x2 = 100 ⇒ x = 10.

d2(AC)/dx2 = 400/x3 > 0 at x = 10 ⇒ minimum.

AC at x = 10 = 20 + 5 + 20 = ₹45. MC = dC/dx = 4x + 5 = ₹45 at x = 10. Hence MC = AC = ₹45 at the minimum-AC output of 10 units.

questions.q: A firm faces the demand function p = 120 − 2x and has cost function C(x) = 100 + 30x + x<sup>2</sup>. Find (a) the profit function, (b) the output and price that maximise profit, (c) the maximum profit, and (d) verify that MR = MC at this output.

Case study. A stationery company makes open gift boxes from square cardboard sheets of side 18 cm by cutting equal squares of side x cm from the four corners and folding up the flaps.
(i) Express the volume V of the box in terms of x and state the domain.
(ii) Find dV/dx.
(iii) Find the value of x that maximises the volume and the maximum volume.
questions.answerHtml:
(i) Base side = 18 − 2x, height = x. V = x(18 − 2x)2 = 4x3 − 72x2 + 324x, with 0 < x < 9.

(ii) dV/dx = 12x2 − 144x + 324 = 12(x2 − 12x + 27) = 12(x − 3)(x − 9).

(iii) dV/dx = 0 ⇒ x = 3 or 9; x = 9 makes the base zero, so reject it. d2V/dx2 = 24x − 144 = −72 < 0 at x = 3 ⇒ maximum.

x = 3 cm; maximum volume = 3 × (12)2 = 432 cm3.
